title: In defence of boredom
text: Boredom has a bad {{1}}, and most of us will do almost anything to avoid it. Given the {{2}} of an empty afternoon, we reach for the phone before the feeling has even properly arrived. That reflex looks modern, but laboratory work has long shown how far people will go to escape their own thoughts: in one famous study, volunteers left alone for fifteen minutes chose to {{3}} themselves with mild electric shocks rather than sit quietly. Psychologists now argue that boredom is not a malfunction but a {{4}}: the mind, denied outside input, begins generating its own. Mind-wandering has been firmly {{5}} to creativity; problems famously crack themselves in showers, on trains and during long walks, precisely when nothing interesting is happening. The smartphone has made boredom {{6}} extinct, and few of us mourn. Yet at the first {{7}} of an idle moment we now scroll, and the mental space where ideas used to form is quietly leased out. The case for boredom is finally practical: guard a little of it, and out of it come some of the mind's best {{8}}.

gaps.explanation: 'has a bad reputation' — the fixed collocation.
'the prospect of an empty afternoon' — the thought of it coming.
'occupy themselves with electric shocks' — occupy oneself with = fill time with.
'not a malfunction but a signal' — it carries information.
'has been linked to creativity' — the standard research collocation.
'made boredom virtually extinct' — adverb of degree.
'at the first twinge of an idle moment' — a small stab of a feeling.
'some of the mind's best inventions' — plural noun needed.
